description: 6 desarrolladores guatemaltecos apasionados por el espacio y la tecnología, listos para convertir los datos abiertos de la NASA en soluciones prácticas y accesibles con impacto real.
summary:
HELIOS.L is a web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a nearby hill can mean night for the solar panels and can hide Earth, cutting direct radio contact.

HELIOS.L combines NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides with LRO LOLA terrain models. For each site it traces the real topographic horizon in 720 directions up to 150 km and shows, hour by hour over a full year, whether the Sun and Earth are visible. Users compare up to three sites at the same date on maps, a site relief with annual sunlight and slope, a 3D terrain lit by the real Sun and a 3D view of the Sun, Earth and Moon. It also finds the next window with both sunlight and Earth contact, and works for any coordinates.

The results show a real trade-off: the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge has sunlight 81% of the year but sees Earth only 51% of the time, while the Malapert massif sees Earth 72% of the time. By showing power and communication together, HELIOS.L helps Artemis-era missions pick safer landing sites and dates.
details:
What it does

HELIOS.L is a web navigator for choosing where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. Near the pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees, so local terrain decides two things a lander needs at once: sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct radio contact. HELIOS.L shows both, hour by hour, for a full year starting 15 November 2026, and lets users compare up to three landing scenarios at the same date.

How it works

1. Ephemerides: NASA JPL Horizons gives the topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth from each site, every hour, plus the sub-solar and sub-Earth points and the Earth–Moon distance.

2. Terrain: LRO LOLA elevation models (LDEM_80S_80M at 80 m for the south pole and LDEM_64 for the rest of the Moon) give the ground around each site.

3. Real horizon: for every site we trace the topographic horizon in 720 directions out to 150 km, including the curvature of the Moon and a 2 m mast height.

4. Visibility: we compute what fraction of the solar disk (0.27° radius) and of Earth's disk (0.95° radius) is above that horizon, instead of a simple yes/no.

5. Metrics: sunlight percentage, Earth-in-view percentage, the longest night, the next window with both Sun and Earth, upcoming sunrise/sunset and earthrise/earthset events, landing slope and permanently shadowed area.

What users can do

- Compare up to 3 sites side by side, all at the same date, or follow the real UTC clock in Live mode.

- Explore a whole-Moon map and a south-pole map with day/night, the Earth-visibility limit and candidate sites.

- Inspect each site's relief (32 × 32 km) with heat maps of annual sunlight and Earth visibility, landing slope and permanent shadow.

- See the 3D terrain lit by the real Sun, and a 3D Sun–Earth–Moon system with the planets in their real positions.

- Read the sky from the site (Sun and Earth paths over the terrain profile), a 30-day timeline, a year comparison and an events list, and download hourly data as CSV.

- Enter any coordinates on the Moon: the horizon and a full year of Sun and Earth visibility are computed in the browser in under a second.

Benefits and intended impact

The results show a real trade-off that a flat-horizon analysis would miss: the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge has sunlight 81% of the year but sees Earth only 51% of the time, while the Malapert massif sees Earth 72% of the time with 54% sunlight. The IM-1 Odysseus site has an 11.5° slope (that lander tipped over in 2024), and the Chang'e 6 site on the far side never sees Earth. By putting power, communication and terrain in one view, HELIOS.L helps Artemis-era planners, students and the public understand why site and date selection matters, and choose safer combinations.

Validation

- Planet positions match JPL Horizons within 1.5 arcminutes.

- For custom coordinates, Sun and Earth elevations match Horizons within 0.02°, and south of 84°S the horizon matches the precomputed 80 m sites within 0.06° on average.

- Each site's heat-map centre was cross-checked against its own hourly series.

Tools and languages

- Rust: offline scientific precompute (horizons, heat maps, relief, slopes, permanent shadow).

- TypeScript with Astro: static website.

- Three.js: 3D views. Leaflet: maps.

- Python: data reduction of the LOLA terrain and textures.

- GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages: free, public hosting with no server.

How it is creative

Instead of a flat horizon, every answer uses the real terrain profile. Power and radio contact are shown together, with the next window when both are available. The site runs entirely in the browser, including custom points, so anyone can use it for free.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy against size: full 80 m terrain near the pole, and lighter models elsewhere, with the resolution shown in the table.

- Partial visibility of the Sun and Earth disks.

- Accessibility (tooltips, keyboard navigation, readable charts) and an English/Spanish interface.
